title: Ownership, ~Copyable and Span
summary: `~Copyable` types cannot be copied - only moved - so the compiler guarantees one owner. `Span` and `InlineArray` give fast, safe access to memory without heap allocation.
body: **In simple words:** Normally Swift copies values freely. Some things should never be copied: a file handle, a one-time payment token, a lock. Marking a type `~Copyable` ("not copyable") makes the compiler enforce one owner at a time.
**Real-life analogy:** A concert ticket that can be handed over but not photocopied. Once you give it away (consume it), you no longer have it.
**Parameter keywords:** `borrowing` = "let me look at it, I will give it back" (no copy). `consuming` = "give it to me, it is mine now".

**Span and InlineArray (Swift 6.2):** `Span` is a safe view over a block of memory (a modern, checked replacement for many unsafe pointers). `InlineArray<4, Int>` is a fixed-size array stored inline, with no heap allocation.
**Who needs this?** Performance-critical code (parsers, image/audio processing) and SDK authors. Most app code does not, but staff candidates should know what these features are for.
keyPoints: `~Copyable` = unique ownership, enforced by the compiler; structs can have `deinit`.
`Span` = safe view over contiguous memory; `InlineArray` = fixed-size, no heap.
`Mutex` is noncopyable because a lock must have one stable address.

code.caption: A single-use token

followups: **Why would you use `~Copyable` in an app?** To model resources that must be used exactly once, e.g. a transaction that must be committed or rolled back.
